anchor.text: Connect café with Finnish kahvila: picture the café counter when you order un café.

coffee.soundFi: Final é is pronounced as a clear e-like vowel; avoid the English diphthong in café.

article.note: Café is masculine. Du café means some coffee; un café normally means one serving.

anchor.text: Thé is the familiar tea word: connect it with Finnish tee and German Tee.

tea.soundFi: The h is silent. Thé has one clear e-like vowel, with no final extra vowel.

article.note: Thé is masculine. Du thé means some tea; un thé can mean one serving.

anchor.text: Picture a jug arriving at your restaurant table: une carafe d’eau. The little word eau names the water.

water.soundFi: The three letters eau make one o-like vowel, a little more closed and rounded than Finnish o.

article.note: Eau is feminine: la becomes l’ before its vowel. For some water say de l’eau; une eau can name a type.

anchor.text: Picture a bread basket beside your plate and ask for du pain. Keep pain with that meal scene.

bread.soundFi: The ain is one nasal vowel. Do not pronounce a separate Finnish n at the end.

article.note: Pain is masculine. For an unspecified amount of bread, use du pain; un pain can mean a loaf.

anchor.text: Use the crescent-shaped pastry you already know as the picture for croissant.

croissant.soundFi: The oi sounds like wa; an is nasal and the final t is silent.

article.note: Croissant is masculine. Learn the pastry together with un croissant.

anchor.text: Menu looks familiar, but here it means a set of courses for one price. La carte is the full list.

set-menu.soundFi: The final u is close to Finnish y, not Finnish u.

article.note: Menu is masculine. Un menu names one set meal; this gender is a property of the noun.

anchor.text: Connect carte with a card: picture the card listing the restaurant’s dishes.

menu.soundFi: The t is pronounced; the final e is silent. Do not add a vowel after the t.

article.note: Carte is feminine. The menu card is une carte; learn article and noun together.

anchor.text: English table gives the meaning directly. Attach the French article: une table.

table.soundFi: Final e is silent. The word ends in bl, without an extra Finnish vowel.

article.note: Table is feminine. Its meaning does not predict its gender; keep une table as one unit.

anchor.text: Imagine the server adding up your meal: ask for l’addition when you are ready to pay.

bill.soundFi: The ending tion has a nasal vowel; do not add a separate Finnish n. Double d is not a long Finnish consonant.

article.note: Addition is feminine, like many nouns in -tion. Before its vowel, la becomes l’.

anchor.text: Connect carafe with English carafe: picture the water jug shared by everyone at the table.

jug.soundFi: The final f is pronounced and the final e is silent.

article.note: Carafe is feminine. Learn une carafe, especially in the chunk une carafe d’eau.

anchor.text: Picture the main plate arriving: le plat du jour is the dish of the day.

dish.soundFi: The final t is silent in plat. The word ends in its vowel.

article.note: Plat is masculine. Learn un plat du jour for one dish of the day.

anchor.text: Dessert matches English dessert. Picture the sweet course after le plat.

dessert.soundFi: The double s is an unvoiced s. The final t is silent; désert has a different, voiced s sound.

article.note: Dessert is masculine. Learn un dessert as the final course of the meal.

anchor.text: Connect végétarien with English vegetarian. For a dish, un plat végétarien means a vegetarian dish.

vegetarian.soundFi: The gé has a voiced zh sound, not Finnish g. The final ien is nasal.

anchor.text: Imagine crossing sugar off a coffee order: un café sans sucre. Put sans before the ingredient to leave out.

without.soundFi: The an is nasal. Neither the n nor the final s is a separate consonant here.

anchor.text: Emporter means to carry away. Picture carrying your cup out of the café: à emporter.

takeaway.soundFi: The em is nasal; final er is pronounced as a clear e-like vowel, without a final r.

anchor.text: Imagine colleagues gathering for talks: le colloque is the whole academic event. La conférence can mean one lecture.

conference.soundFi: The final que is a k sound; its u and e are not separate vowels.

article.note: Colloque is masculine. Learn un colloque for one academic event.

anchor.text: Connect présentation with Finnish presentaatio and English presentation; picture yourself beside your slides.

presentation.soundFi: The ending tion has a nasal vowel, without a separate Finnish n.

article.note: Présentation is feminine, like many nouns ending in -tion.

anchor.text: Badge matches English badge: picture the name label hanging from a conference lanyard.

badge.soundFi: Keep the voiced dge sound of English badge; do not add a final Finnish vowel.

article.note: Badge is masculine in French. Its gender must be learned with the word.

anchor.text: Think of writing your name on the conference list: inscription. The ending -tion often marks an action noun.

registration.soundFi: The initial in and final on are nasal vowels; neither needs a separate Finnish n.

article.note: Inscription is feminine, like many nouns ending in -tion. La becomes l’ before its vowel.

anchor.text: Picture the room number on a conference door: la salle is the room or hall, not a hotel bedroom.

meeting-room.soundFi: The ll does not make a long Finnish l here. Final e is silent.

article.note: Salle is feminine. Keep une salle for a room or hall; une chambre is a bedroom.

anchor.text: Connect pause with Finnish paussi and German Pause. Picture leaving the lecture room for coffee.

break.soundFi: The au is o-like; the s is voiced z, unlike the s in Finnish paussi.

article.note: Pause is feminine. Learn une pause café, a coffee break.

anchor.text: Question matches English question. Picture raising a hand: j’ai une question.

question.soundFi: The qu is k. Say the t in question; final on is nasal without a separate Finnish n.

article.note: Question is feminine, like many nouns ending in -tion. Learn une question as a unit.

anchor.text: Connect réponse with English response. Picture the speaker answering your raised hand.

answer.soundFi: The on is nasal. The final se has an s sound, not z.

article.note: Réponse is feminine. The gender belongs to the noun, not to who answers.

anchor.text: See chercher, “to look for”, inside recherche: research means looking for knowledge.

research.soundFi: Both ch groups have a sh sound. Final e is silent.

article.note: Recherche is feminine. In this field-of-work sense, say de la recherche rather than une recherche.

anchor.text: Connect domaine with English domain: picture a label naming the area of your research.

field.soundFi: Here ai is e-like and the n is pronounced; the following e prevents the nasal reading.

article.note: Domaine is masculine. Its final -e does not make it feminine; learn un domaine.

anchor.text: Programme matches English programme. Picture the printed timetable listing each conference session.

programme.soundFi: Double m is not a long Finnish consonant here; final e is silent.

article.note: Programme is masculine despite its final -e. Learn un programme as a unit.

anchor.text: Picture your research poster fixed to the wall by the entrance: mon affiche.

poster.soundFi: The ch is sh. Final e is silent, and ff is not a long Finnish f.

article.note: Affiche is feminine: la becomes l’ before its vowel. Une affiche shows its gender clearly.

anchor.text: English university and German Universität give you a direct bridge to université.

university.soundFi: The initial u is close to Finnish y. Final é is pronounced.

article.note: Université is feminine. Many abstract nouns in -té are feminine; the pattern has exceptions.

anchor.text: Chercher means to look for. A chercheur is a person who searches for knowledge; chercheuse is the feminine form.

researcher.soundFi: The ch is sh; eu is near Finnish ö, with a more open French vowel here.

article.note: Chercheur is the masculine form; une chercheuse is the feminine form. Learn each noun with its article.

anchor.text: Connect discuter with English discuss or Finnish diskuteerata: picture talking about a poster during the break.

chat.soundFi: The u is close to Finnish y. Final er is e-like, without a final r.

anchor.text: Use the timetable anchor: déjeuner is the meal around midi, noon. Petit déjeuner is breakfast.

lunch.soundFi: The j is voiced zh, not Finnish j. Final er is e-like and its r is silent.

article.note: Déjeuner is masculine as a meal noun. Here un déjeuner is one lunch.

anchor.text: Connect dîner with English dinner; picture the evening meal after the last conference session.

dinner.soundFi: The î is an i vowel; its accent does not mean a Finnish double vowel. Final r is silent.

article.note: Dîner is masculine as a meal noun. Here un dîner is one dinner.

anchor.text: Connect serveur with English server: picture the person bringing la carte to your table.

restaurant-server.soundFi: The eu is an ö-like vowel; keep the final r audible.

article.note: Serveur is the masculine form. The feminine form is une serveuse.

anchor.text: Boulanger is a baker; boulangerie is the baker’s shop. The ending -erie often names a shop or activity.

bakery.soundFi: The ou is close to Finnish u; an is nasal and g before e has a voiced zh sound.

article.note: Boulangerie is feminine. The -erie ending often appears in feminine shop and activity nouns.

anchor.text: Restaurant is familiar from English and German. Picture the sign above the place where you eat.

restaurant.soundFi: The au is o-like and an is nasal. The final t is silent.

article.note: Restaurant is masculine. Learn un restaurant as the name of one place to eat.

anchor.text: Picture ordering while standing at the café counter: on commande au comptoir.

counter.soundFi: The p is silent. The oi is wa-like, and the final r is pronounced.

article.note: Comptoir is masculine. Keep le comptoir with the useful location chunk au comptoir.

anchor.text: Terrasse connects directly with Finnish terassi: picture outdoor tables in an Angers square.

terrace.soundFi: Double s keeps an unvoiced s sound. Final e is silent.

article.note: Terrasse is feminine. Learn une terrasse as an outdoor seating area.

anchor.text: Picture a transparent glass beside the water jug: un verre d’eau. Keep verre with that object.

drinking-glass.soundFi: The final e is silent; rr is not a long Finnish consonant here.

article.note: Verre is masculine despite final -e. Un verre d’eau is one glass of water.

anchor.text: Connect tasse with German Tasse: picture the cup with a handle under your espresso.

cup.soundFi: The double s is an unvoiced s. Final e is silent.

article.note: Tasse is feminine. Keep une tasse with the cup image.

anchor.text: Picture your meal sitting on the round plate: l’assiette. Contrast it with le plat, the dish itself.

plate.soundFi: The final t is pronounced; final e is silent. Double t does not mean a long Finnish t.

article.note: Assiette is feminine: la becomes l’ before its vowel. Une assiette makes the gender visible.

anchor.text: Imagine the fork’s prongs on the left of your plate: une fourchette.

fork.soundFi: The ou is near Finnish u, ch is sh, and the final t is pronounced.

article.note: Fourchette is feminine. Nouns ending in -ette are often feminine, but endings are tendencies.

anchor.text: Picture cutting a bread roll with the knife: le couteau beside your plate.

knife.soundFi: The ou is close to Finnish u. The letters eau make one o-like vowel.

article.note: Couteau is masculine. Nouns ending in -eau are often masculine; l’eau is a useful exception.

anchor.text: Picture a spoon lifting soup to your mouth: une cuillère pour la soupe.

spoon.soundFi: The u starts near Finnish y; ill contains a Finnish j-like glide. The final r is pronounced.

article.note: Cuillère is feminine. Learn une cuillère as a whole phrase.

anchor.text: Serviette alone can mean a towel. De table, “of the table”, makes it the napkin beside your plate.

napkin.soundFi: In serviette, tt gives one t here. Final e is silent in both serviette and table.

article.note: Serviette is feminine. Adding de table does not change the gender of the main noun.

anchor.text: Imagine the small salt shaker beside the pepper: le sel. Say avec du sel when adding some salt.

salt.soundFi: Keep the final l audible; do not add an extra vowel after it.

article.note: Sel is masculine. For some salt, use du sel; un sel would mean a kind of salt.

anchor.text: Picture turning the pepper mill over your meal: du poivre. Contrast it with le sel.

pepper.soundFi: The oi is wa-like. The v is pronounced; final e is silent.

article.note: Poivre is masculine. For some pepper, use du poivre; un poivre can mean a variety.

anchor.text: Sucre echoes Finnish sokeri. Picture a sugar cube beside your coffee and the phrase sans sucre, without sugar.

sugar.soundFi: The u is close to Finnish y, not Finnish u. Final e is silent.

article.note: Sucre is masculine. For some sugar, use du sucre; un sucre can mean a sugar cube.

anchor.text: Picture a small milk jug beside the coffee cup: un peu de lait.

milk.soundFi: The ai is an open e-like vowel. The final t is silent.

article.note: Lait is masculine. For some milk, use du lait; un lait may name a type or serving.

anchor.text: Picture a cube of butter melting into warm bread: du pain avec du beurre. Tie beurre to that breakfast scene.

butter.soundFi: The eu is an open ö-like vowel. Final e is silent and rr is not Finnish double r.

article.note: Beurre is masculine. For some butter, use du beurre; un beurre can mean a type.

anchor.text: Picture the cheese board after a French meal: du fromage. Keep the word with that course.

cheese.soundFi: The final ge has a voiced zh sound; its e is not a separate vowel.

article.note: Fromage is masculine. -age is often masculine, with exceptions. Du fromage means some cheese.

anchor.text: Picture one egg on a breakfast plate: un œuf. The singular object gives you a firm visual anchor.

egg.soundFi: The œu is an open ö-like vowel, and the f is pronounced in this singular form.

article.note: Œuf is masculine: le becomes l’ before its vowel. Un œuf shows the gender clearly.

anchor.text: Picture the chicken dish on a menu: le poulet avec du riz.

chicken.soundFi: The ou is close to Finnish u. Final et is e-like and the t is silent.

article.note: Poulet is masculine. Du poulet means some chicken meat; un poulet is a whole chicken.

anchor.text: Picture a fish on the restaurant’s menu: le poisson du jour.

fish.soundFi: The oi is wa-like, ss is unvoiced s, and on is nasal. Poison with one s has a voiced z.

article.note: Poisson is masculine. Du poisson means some fish; un poisson means an individual fish.

anchor.text: Picture the meat section of a menu; je ne mange pas de viande is the useful refusal chunk.

meat.soundFi: The an is nasal. The final d is pronounced, while final e is silent.

article.note: Viande is feminine. For some meat, say de la viande rather than une viande.

anchor.text: Picture a colourful vegetable side dish: des légumes avec le plat.

vegetables.soundFi: The u is close to Finnish y. The final plural s is silent.

article.note: Légume is masculine; légumes is plural. Les/des are plural articles and do not reveal gender by themselves.

anchor.text: Salade connects directly with Finnish salaatti. Picture the salad bowl or a light lunch.

salad.soundFi: Keep the final d audible; final e is silent.

article.note: Salade is feminine. Une salade can mean a prepared salad or one serving.

anchor.text: Connect soupe with German Suppe: picture a warm soup bowl and spoon.

soup.soundFi: The ou is close to Finnish u. The p is audible and final e is silent.

article.note: Soupe is feminine. De la soupe means some soup; une soupe can mean one serving or kind.

anchor.text: Riz connects with Finnish riisi and German Reis. Picture the small grains beside your main dish.

rice.soundFi: The word ends in its i vowel: the final z is silent.

article.note: Riz is masculine. For an unspecified amount of rice, use du riz rather than un riz.

anchor.text: Picture several strands of pasta on a plate. French normally uses the plural: des pâtes.

pasta.soundFi: The t is pronounced and the final plural s is silent. The accent is not a Finnish length mark.

article.note: Pâte is feminine; pâtes is normally plural for pasta. Use les pâtes or des pâtes.

anchor.text: Pomme de terre literally gives “apple of the earth”: picture a potato coming out of the soil.

potato.soundFi: Final e is silent in pomme and terre; the written double consonants are not Finnish long consonants.

article.note: Pomme is feminine. The phrase de terre does not change the main noun’s gender.

anchor.text: Picture an apple beside a potato: pomme is the apple; pomme de terre is the potato.

apple.soundFi: The m is pronounced, but mm does not make a long Finnish m here. Final e is silent.

article.note: Pomme is feminine. Learn une pomme and connect it with une pomme de terre.

anchor.text: Picture an orange squeezed into a breakfast glass: un jus d’orange.

juice.soundFi: The u is close to Finnish y. The final s is silent.

article.note: Jus is masculine. Du jus means some juice; un jus is commonly one serving.

anchor.text: Bière connects with German Bier. Picture ordering a local beer: une bière locale.

beer.soundFi: The i leads into a Finnish j-like glide; è is an open e-like vowel, and the final r is audible.

article.note: Bière is feminine. De la bière means some beer; une bière can mean one serving.

anchor.text: Connect vin with Finnish viini. Picture a wine glass and the phrase un verre de vin.

wine.soundFi: The in is one nasal vowel. Do not pronounce a separate Finnish n.

article.note: Vin is masculine. Du vin means some wine; un vin can mean a particular wine.

anchor.text: Picture a whole bottle shared by the table: une bouteille d’eau. Contrast it with one verre.

bottle.soundFi: The ou is close to Finnish u; the ending ille has a Finnish j-like sound.

article.note: Bouteille is feminine. Une bouteille d’eau keeps the gender of bouteille, the container.

anchor.text: Connect gazeuse with gas: picture bubbles rising in the water. It contrasts with eau plate.

sparkling-water.soundFi: The s in gazeuse is voiced z. The eu is a rounded ö-like vowel.

article.note: Eau is feminine. Gazeuse agrees with it; for some sparkling water say de l’eau gazeuse.

anchor.text: Picture a flat, bubble-free surface: eau plate is still water. The “flat” picture is a memory association.

still-water.soundFi: The t in plate is pronounced, unlike the silent t in plat. Final e is silent.

article.note: Eau is feminine. Plate agrees with it; for some still water say de l’eau plate.

anchor.text: Portion matches English portion and Finnish annos: picture one measured serving on a plate.

portion.soundFi: The ending tion has a nasal vowel, without a separate Finnish n.

article.note: Portion is feminine, like many nouns ending in -tion. Learn une portion.

anchor.text: Pair the noun commande with the verb commander: your restaurant order is what you ask the kitchen to prepare.

food-order.soundFi: The an is nasal and the final d is pronounced. Double m is not a long Finnish consonant.

article.note: Commande is feminine. It is the noun paired with the verb commander.

anchor.text: Pair commander with la commande, the order. Picture telling the server which dish you want.

order-food.soundFi: The an is nasal. Final er is e-like, without a pronounced final r.

anchor.text: Connect payer with English pay. Picture handing over your bank card: je voudrais payer.

pay.soundFi: The middle y has a Finnish j-like sound. Final er is pronounced e-like, without r.

anchor.text: You already know carte as a card. Bancaire tells you this one belongs to the bank, not the restaurant menu.

bank-card.soundFi: The an in bancaire is nasal, without a separate Finnish n. The final r is pronounced.

article.note: Carte is feminine. Bancaire describes the card and does not change its gender.

anchor.text: Picture coins and notes in your hand: payer en espèces. Learn the payment chunk, not “species”.

cash.soundFi: The c before è is an s sound. The final plural s is silent.

article.note: Espèces is feminine plural in the cash expression. Learn payer en espèces; un/une does not fit this meaning.

anchor.text: Séparée resembles English separated: picture one bill for each person instead of a shared total.

separate-bill.soundFi: The final ée is a pronounced e-like vowel. The ending tion is nasal without a separate Finnish n.

article.note: Addition is feminine. Séparée agrees with it; la becomes l’ before its vowel.

anchor.text: Place can mean a place. Picture keeping your cup at the café: sur place contrasts with à emporter.

eat-in.soundFi: The u is close to Finnish y. Final e in place is silent.

anchor.text: Conférence resembles English conference, but here it is one lecture or talk. Le colloque is the whole academic event.

lecture.soundFi: The on and en are different nasal vowels; neither needs a separate Finnish n.

article.note: Conférence is feminine. The -ence ending is often feminine; here the word means a lecture or talk.

anchor.text: Session connects with Finnish sessio: picture one block of talks on the conference timetable.

session.soundFi: The double s stays unvoiced; final ion ends in a nasal vowel.

article.note: Session is feminine, like many nouns ending in -sion. Learn une session.

anchor.text: Picture a small group doing an activity around a table: un atelier rather than a large lecture.

workshop.soundFi: The ending ier has a Finnish j-like glide followed by an e-like vowel; final r is silent.

article.note: Atelier is masculine: le becomes l’ before its vowel. Un atelier shows the gender.

anchor.text: Réunion contains the idea of coming together again: picture colleagues gathering around a meeting table.

meeting.soundFi: The u is close to Finnish y; the final ion ends in a nasal vowel.

article.note: Réunion is feminine, like many nouns ending in -ion. Learn une réunion.

anchor.text: Séminaire connects directly with Finnish seminaari and German Seminar.

seminar.soundFi: The ai is e-like; the n and final r are pronounced here.

article.note: Séminaire is masculine despite its final -e. Learn un séminaire.

anchor.text: Intervenir means to intervene or contribute. Picture the person contributing the talk at the microphone.

speaker.soundFi: Initial in and final an are nasal vowels. The final t is silent.

article.note: Intervenant is the masculine form; une intervenante is the feminine form.

anchor.text: Connect public with the public: picture everyone seated facing the speaker. Here it names the audience.

audience.soundFi: The u is close to Finnish y. The final c is pronounced as k.

article.note: Public is masculine as a collective noun. It stays le public regardless of the people in the audience.

anchor.text: Participant matches English participant. Picture each attendee collecting a badge at registration.

attendee.soundFi: The final ant is nasal, without a separate Finnish n. The final t is silent.

article.note: Participant is the masculine form; une participante is the feminine form.

anchor.text: Organisateur connects with Finnish organisaattori: picture the person answering questions at the conference desk.

organizer.soundFi: The s between vowels is voiced z. The ending eur has an ö-like vowel and an audible r.

article.note: Organisateur is the masculine form; une organisatrice is the feminine form.

anchor.text: Collègue connects directly with Finnish kollega and German Kollege. Picture the person from your own team.

colleague.soundFi: The gu gives a hard g; u is not a separate vowel here. Final e is silent.

article.note: Collègue can describe any gender: un collègue or une collègue. The noun’s spelling stays the same.

anchor.text: Picture a student introducing their university: je suis étudiant à Angers.

student.soundFi: The u is close to Finnish y and final ant is nasal. The final t is silent.

article.note: Étudiant is the masculine form; une étudiante is the feminine form.

anchor.text: Professeur connects directly with Finnish professori. In other contexts it can also mean a teacher.

professor.soundFi: The ss is unvoiced s. The final eur has an ö-like vowel and an audible r.

article.note: The listed form is le professeur. For a woman, la professeure is common; la professeur is also used.

anchor.text: Laboratoire connects directly with Finnish laboratorio: picture your research group’s workplace.

laboratory.soundFi: The ending oire is wa-like followed by r; final e is silent.

article.note: Laboratoire is masculine despite final -e. Learn un laboratoire.

anchor.text: Picture your colleagues grouped together on a project: notre équipe. Keep the word with that group picture.

team.soundFi: The qu is k, without a u vowel. Final e is silent.

article.note: Équipe is feminine: la becomes l’ before its vowel. Une équipe makes the gender visible.

anchor.text: Projet connects with Finnish projekti and English project. Picture a named folder containing your research plans.

project.soundFi: The j is voiced zh, not Finnish j. The final t is silent.

article.note: Projet is masculine. Learn un projet with the familiar project meaning.

anchor.text: Connect sujet with English subject: picture the one topic written at the top of a presentation.

topic.soundFi: The u is close to Finnish y, j is voiced zh, and the final t is silent.

article.note: Sujet is masculine. Learn un sujet for the topic under discussion.

anchor.text: Connect titre with English title: picture the large heading on the first slide or paper.

title.soundFi: The word ends in tr, without an extra Finnish vowel; final e is silent.

article.note: Titre is masculine despite final -e. Learn un titre as a unit.

anchor.text: Résumé means the summary of the paper here. Picture the short paragraph before the full research article.

abstract.soundFi: The s between vowels is voiced z. Both written é vowels are pronounced.

article.note: Résumé is masculine as a noun. Learn un résumé for one summary or abstract.

anchor.text: Article connects directly with Finnish artikkeli. Picture a paper with authors, an abstract and references.

scientific-paper.soundFi: The c is a k sound; final e is silent. Do not add a vowel after the final l.

article.note: Article is masculine: le becomes l’ before its vowel. Un article shows its gender.

anchor.text: Résultat connects with English result: picture the outcome column in your experiment.

result.soundFi: The u is close to Finnish y. The s is voiced z and the final t is silent.

article.note: Résultat is masculine. Learn un résultat for one outcome.

anchor.text: Méthode connects directly with Finnish metodi. Picture the “Methods” section of a research paper.

method.soundFi: The th is simply t, not English th. The final d is pronounced and final e is silent.

article.note: Méthode is feminine despite the familiar English/German-looking form. Learn une méthode.

anchor.text: Donner means to give; données are the given information. Picture the rows of measurements in your dataset.

data.soundFi: The ending ées is one e-like vowel; final s is silent. Double n is not a long Finnish n.

article.note: Donnée is feminine; données is plural. Les/des do not reveal gender, so remember une donnée too.

anchor.text: Expérience resembles English experience, but in this scientific example it means an experiment. Picture a lab test.

experiment.soundFi: The x is ks. The en is nasal and final ce has an s sound.

article.note: Expérience is feminine: la becomes l’ before its vowel. Une expérience shows the gender.

anchor.text: Analyse connects directly with Finnish analyysi. Picture studying the measurements after an experiment.

analysis.soundFi: The written y is an i sound, not Finnish y. The s is voiced z.

article.note: Analyse is feminine: la becomes l’ before its vowel. Une analyse shows the gender.

anchor.text: Conclusion matches English conclusion: picture the final statement that follows from the results.

conclusion.soundFi: The u is close to Finnish y; s is voiced z, and final ion ends in a nasal vowel.

article.note: Conclusion is feminine, like many nouns ending in -sion. Learn une conclusion.

anchor.text: Source matches English source: picture an arrow leading from a claim back to its original information.

source.soundFi: The ou is close to Finnish u. Final ce has an s sound.

article.note: Source is feminine. Learn une source for one source of information.

anchor.text: Référence connects with English reference. Picture the author and year beside a claim in your paper.

reference.soundFi: Final ence has a nasal vowel followed by s, without a separate Finnish n.

article.note: Référence is feminine. The -ence ending is often feminine, but endings are tendencies.

anchor.text: Graphique connects with Finnish grafiikka and English graph. Picture results plotted on two axes.

graph.soundFi: The ph is f and qu is k. Final e is silent.

article.note: Graphique is masculine as this noun, even though it ends in -e. Learn un graphique.

anchor.text: Diapositive connects with Finnish dia. Picture one slide on the screen behind a speaker.

slide.soundFi: The final v is pronounced; final e is silent. Keep i as an i vowel.

article.note: Diapositive is feminine. Its everyday shortened form is also feminine: une diapo.

anchor.text: Picture the screen everyone is looking at during a talk: l’écran. It can also be your computer screen.

screen.soundFi: Initial é is pronounced; an is nasal without a separate Finnish n.

article.note: Écran is masculine: le becomes l’ before its vowel. Un écran shows its gender.

anchor.text: Micro is the everyday short form of microphone: connect it with Finnish mikrofoni.

microphone.soundFi: The i is like Finnish i; keep final o rounded and do not add an extra vowel.

article.note: Micro is masculine, like the full noun microphone. Learn un micro.

anchor.text: Projecteur connects with Finnish projektori. Picture the device sending your slides onto the screen.

projector.soundFi: The j is voiced zh; final eur has an ö-like vowel and an audible r.

article.note: Projecteur is masculine. Device nouns in -eur are often masculine, but -eur alone is not a universal rule.

anchor.text: Câble connects with Finnish kaapeli and English cable. Picture the lead joining your laptop to the projector.

cable.soundFi: Final e is silent. The accent on â is not an instruction to copy Finnish double-vowel spelling.

article.note: Câble is masculine despite final -e. Learn un câble with the cable image.

anchor.text: Picture the wall socket where you can plug in your charger: une prise près de la table.

socket.soundFi: The s between vowels is voiced z; final e is silent.

article.note: Prise is feminine. Learn une prise for one electrical socket.

anchor.text: Picture your laptop inside your conference bag: mon ordinateur. Keep the word with your own device.

computer.soundFi: Final eur has an ö-like vowel and an audible r. The final r is not silent here.

article.note: Ordinateur is masculine: le becomes l’ before its vowel. Un ordinateur shows its gender.

anchor.text: Picture a clickable connection between two webpages: le lien that someone sends after a talk.

link.soundFi: The i leads into a Finnish j-like glide; final en is nasal without a separate Finnish n.

article.note: Lien is masculine. Learn un lien for one connection or web link.

anchor.text: Site web connects directly with English website. Picture the conference homepage with its programme.

website.soundFi: The w in web is a w sound, not Finnish v. The final b is voiced and audible.

article.note: Site is masculine. Adding web does not change the main noun’s gender.

anchor.text: Courriel combines French courrier, mail, and électronique. Picture sending your follow-up message after the conference.

email.soundFi: The ou is close to Finnish u; the ending iel has a Finnish j-like glide and an audible l.

article.note: Courriel is masculine. Learn un courriel for one email message.

anchor.text: You know carte, a card. De visite identifies the little card you give a new professional contact.

business-card.soundFi: The s in visite is voiced z; the final e is silent.

article.note: Carte is feminine. The added phrase de visite does not change its gender.

anchor.text: Connect rendez-vous with German Rendezvous. Picture a calendar entry reserved for an agreed meeting.

appointment.soundFi: The ez ends in an e-like vowel. The ou is close to Finnish u and final s is silent.

article.note: Rendez-vous is masculine. Its written ending stays -vous even for one appointment.

anchor.text: Date matches English date. Picture circling one day on the conference calendar.

date.soundFi: The final t is pronounced and final e is silent.

article.note: Date is feminine. Learn une date as one calendar date.

anchor.text: Picture one empty block in a busy timetable: un créneau disponible is an available time slot.

time-slot.soundFi: The ending eau is one rounded o-like vowel. Do not pronounce three separate vowels.

article.note: Créneau is masculine. The ending -eau often appears in masculine nouns.

anchor.text: Pair durée with durer, to last. Picture a timer showing how long your presentation will take.

duration.soundFi: The u is close to Finnish y. Final ée is a pronounced e-like vowel.

article.note: Durée is feminine. Learn une durée for a length of time.

anchor.text: Pair présenter with la présentation. Picture yourself introducing a project while standing beside your slides.

present.soundFi: The s is voiced z, en is nasal, and final er is e-like without a final r.

anchor.text: Picture pressing Send on the message containing your slides: je peux vous envoyer le lien.

send.soundFi: Initial en is nasal; the middle oy includes a Finnish j-like glide. Final er has no pronounced r.
